paper_title: SWE-Duel: Towards a Self-Scaling Arena for Coding Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Static coding benchmarks are fixed at release. Over time their tasks leak into training data, and stronger agents eventually saturate them. We argue that a benchmark should instead aim to be self-scaling: its tasks and oracles are created at evaluation time, so no content exists in advance to leak, and its difficulty is set by the participating agents rather than fixed at release. We introduce SWE-Duel, an arena in which two coding agents evaluate each other over mirrored Red-Blue turns. In each turn, the Red agent works on a real repository across three context-isolated sessions. It proposes and implements a new feature with feature tests, then embeds a subtle bug in that feature along with sealed bug-triggering tests. The resulting pull request is admitted only if (1) it passes the feature tests and the repository's existing tests while failing exactly the bug tests, and (2) a fresh session of the same agent can repair the bug blind, which rules out unsolvable tasks. The Blue agent then reviews the pull request without being told a bug exists. It wins only if its revision passes all three test suites, and then the two agents swap roles. We run a tournament among 11 model-harness participants on 15 repositories in five languages for 1,500 turns. The leaders win in different ways. GPT-5.5 with Codex CLI ranks first as the strongest solver, repairing 98.3% of the defects it reviews. Claude Opus 4.8 with mini-swe-agent ranks second as the strongest task author, with a 27.3% Red win rate. Finally, within one model family, tasks written by the newest version defeat a fixed-reference solver far more often than those of older versions (42.9% vs. 4.0%), giving preliminary evidence that task difficulty scales with task authoring capability.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Benchmarks are the primary instrument for measuring progress in coding agents. To deliver trustworthy signal over the long run, benchmark must remain absent from the training data of the models it evaluates and challenging for agents to solve. This is increasingly difficult to satisfy, as LLMs continually learn from publicly available materials and grow more capable with every generation. The deeper issue is that most existing coding benchmarks are static once released and built from openly accessible sources. Such content is eventually absorbed into training corpora, and fixed task set is eventually saturated by stronger agents. In other words, from the moment benchmark is released, it begins to leak into training data and to fall behind the agents it is meant to measure. We argue that avoiding this consequence requires benchmark to be self-scaling: its tasks and oracles are created at evaluation time, so no content exists in advance to leak, and its difficulty is set by the participating agents rather than fixed at release, so it can rise as those agents improve. Existing benchmarks fall short of this property in different ways. Static benchmarks have already run into this problem: OpenAI recently stopped reporting results on SWE-bench Verified (Jimenez et al., 2024) after finding that frontier models could reproduce its gold patches. Continuously updated benchmarks such as SWE-bench-Live (Zhang et al., 2025) and SWE-rebench (Badertdinov et al., 2025) mitigate leakage by collecting tasks created after model training cutoffs, but their task difficulty is still bounded by the daily issues faced by human developers. Most recently, modelgenerated tasks have emerged as new direction: BugPilot (Sonwane et al., 2025) collects bugs introduced unintentionally by agents implementing new features, and SwingArena (Xu et al., 2026) pairs LLMs as patch submitters and test-writing reviewers in an adversarial arena. However, BugPilot generates its tasks ahead of time as fixed set and SwingArena still draws tasks from fixed pool of human-written GitHub issues, generating only the oracles at evaluation time; neither produces tasks whose difficulty grows with the agent being evaluated. This motivates the central question of this work: Can we create self-scaling benchmark for coding agents? To answer this question, we present SWE-DUEL, self-scaling arena with evaluation protocol in which two coding agents evaluate each other over mirrored adversarial turns. In each turn, the Red agent, working on given repository across three context-isolated sessions, proposes new feature, implements it together with feature tests, and finally injects subtle bugs along with bug-triggering tests. The resulting PR is used in the duel only if 1) it passes the feature tests and the repositorys regression tests while failing exactly the bug-triggering tests, and 2) the Red agent can repair its own bugs in fresh session, which rules out unsolvable tasks. The Blue agent then reviews the PR and submits revision, winning the round if and only if the revision passes all three test suites; the two agents swap roles in the next turn. Because every feature, bug, and oracle is created at evaluation time, these specific tasks cannot appear in earlier training data, And because tasks are authored by the agents under evaluation, task difficulty is not fixed by human-written pool; it can in principle rise as the authors improve, up to the limit set by the self-repair gate. Altogether, single duel profiles broad slice of the software engineering lifecycle, including requirement specification, feature implementation, test generation, code review, fault localization, and program repair. We evaluate SWE-DUEL in tournament among 11 participants, each pairing frontier proprietary or open-weight model (e.g., GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8, DeepSeek V4 Pro, and Gemini 3.1 Pro) with one of three agent harnesses, on 15 repositories in five languages. Ten participants play full round robin, and Gemini 3.1 Pro joins afterwards as late entrant, giving 50 matches and 1,500 turns. The leaders win in different ways. GPT-5.5 with Codex CLI ranks first as the strongest solver, repairing 98.3% of the defects it reviews, while Claude Opus 4.8 with mini-swe-agent ranks second as the strongest task author, with 27.3% Red win rate. late entrant can be placed with only five matches, and within one model family, tasks written by the newest version defeat fixed reviewer far more often than those of older versions (42.9% vs. 4.0%), giving preliminary evidence that difficulty tracks authoring capability. We make the following contributions: We introduce SWE-DUEL, self-scaling arena that evaluates coding agents with each other. It does not leak test content by design and determines the task difficulty with the participants own authoring ability rather than fixed at release. 2 Under review as conference paper at ICLR 2027 Figure 2: contamination-resistant evaluation in SWE-DUEL. Red agent implements new feature with an embedded bug, so that the Blue agent cannot simply revert the repository to its original version to remove the bug as doing so would remove the implemented feature. Feature retention is deterministically verified with the feature test suite, while bug removal is deterministically verified with the bug test suite. Existing test suite verifies no regression by the Blue agents patch. We build an open arena toolkit for SWE-DUEL (Minn, 2026c), enabling the community to start their own tournament from scratch, or add new agent to the existing leaderboard (Minn, 2026b). We conduct 1,500-turn tournament over 11 (model, harness) pairs, demonstrating the broad applicability of SWE-DUEL and revealing distinct behavioral profiles across models and harnesses (Minn, 2026a).

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Repository-level coding benchmarks. SWE-bench (Jimenez et al., 2024; OpenAI, 2024) moved evaluation from isolated functions to real issue resolution. Later benchmarks add automated environment setup (Vergopoulos et al., 2025), more languages (Rashid et al., 2025), long-horizon software evolution (Le et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026), the full issue-resolution cycle (Guan et al., 2026b), and feature addition (Liu et al., 2026). In all of them, the tasks and reference patches are public and fixed before evaluation. However, public tasks eventually enter training data of evaluated LLMs (Matton et al., 2024). The benchmarks thus need to be repeatedly updated to replace the leaked ones. For example, SWE-bench-Live (Zhang et al., 2025) and SWE-rebench (Badertdinov et al., 2025) regularly collect new tasks from GitHub to remain temporally fresh. (Guan et al., 2026a) and DyCodeEval (Chen et al., 2025) propose to perturb the tasks to avoid exact memorization, but preserve the original tasks and solutions. Moreover, the tasks come from human development history (issues, pull requests, and releases), so their difficulty is fixed at release, and fixed task set is saturated as agents improve. The usual response is to build harder benchmark, such as SWE-Bench Pro (Deng et al., 2025), but each replacement again has fixed difficulty. Refreshing the benchmark does not solve this as the new tasks come from the same distribution, so the tasks are newer but not harder. In SWE-Duel, both the tasks and their oracles are written at evaluation time by the agents being evaluated. No task exists in advance to leak, and difficulty is set by the participants instead of fixed human-written pool. Automatic bug generation. Early work injects bugs with predefined or learned patterns: symbolic synthesis of deep faults (Roy et al., 2018), bug seeding learned from past fixes (Patra & Pradel, 2021), learned contextual mutations (Richter & Wehrheim, 2022), and re-introducing fixed security bugs (Zhang & Patterson, 2022). These methods show that realistic bugs can be generated automatically, but each bug is local edit drawn from pattern set, so the variety of bugs is limited by the patterns. LLMs remove this limit. SWE-smith (Yang et al., 2025) prompts LLMs to modify or rewrite functions, BugPilot (Sonwane et al., 2025) collects the regressions that agents cause by accident while adding features, and Self-play SWE-RL (Wei et al., 2025) trains one model to both inject and repair bugs. Both target training data, and they show that LLMs can produce diverse and hard 3 Under review as conference paper at ICLR 2027 bugs at scale. BugPilot is the closest to our task construction, since its bugs also arise while an agent adds feature. The key difference is what the solver can see. BugPilot bug is kept only if it breaks existing tests, so running the test suite reveals it. SWE-DUEL bug is admitted only if all visible tests still pass, so the solver has to find it by reading the code, and only sealed test can confirm the fix. Our bugs are also deliberate, so the task yield does not depend on agents making mistakes, which may become rarer as agents get more reliable. For evaluation, CDBench (Romazanov et al., 2026) lets an attacker LLM write mutants for defender LLM, but the mutants are local edits and the defender is shown the mutant diff. In SWE-DUEL, each agent hides bug inside new feature for the other to fix, and task is admitted only after fresh session of its author repairs the bug blind, so every task is known to be solvable. Arena-style evaluation. Chatbot Arena (Chiang et al., 2024) ranks LLMs from pairwise human votes, and Arena-Lite (Son et al., 2025) and Auto-Arena (Zhao et al., 2025) replace human voters with LLM judges and tournament schedules. Arenas stay fresh because new prompts keep arriving, but their outcomes depend on judges, whose preferences are noisy and are not the same as correctness. SwingArena (Xu et al., 2026) brings the arena format to software engineering and lets repository CI decide the outcome: submitters patch GitHub issues and reviewers write tests. However, its tasks come from fixed pool of human-written issues, and reviewer tests are validated against human gold patch. SWE-DUEL keeps execution-based scoring but removes both human anchors: the competing agents write the tasks themselves, and task validity is checked by execution gates and blind self-repair instead of gold patch. As result, task difficulty is set by the participants and not by human-written pool.

sections.title: 3 SWE-DUEL: A SELF-SCALING CODING ARENA
sections.content: SWE-DUEL evaluates coding agents through RedBlue duels (Figure 2). duel is played by two participants on real repository R, and each participant plays both roles in turn. The Red side creates task which is pull request that adds new feature to and hides bug inside that feature. The Blue side solves the task by reviewing the pull request and submits fixed version if the bug is noticed. Formally, task is tuple = (R, s, d, Tf , Tb), where is the feature specification, is the pullrequest diff that contains both the feature and the bug, Tf is feature test suite, and Tb is bug test suite that fails on only because of the bug. Blue receives only the public part, pub(C) = (R, s, d, Tf ). Tb stays sealed, so Blue is not told whether or where bug exists. Blue returns revised diff and wins the turn if and only if the repositorys existing tests Te, the feature tests Tf , and the sealed bug tests Tb all pass on d; otherwise Red wins. Because the bug lives inside the feature, Blue cannot win by reverting the pull request, since Tf would then fail. Reds tasks are created and validated before the tournament and stored in task bank (Section 3.2), so every opponent faces the same tasks from given Red. In match, the two participants defend each others banked tasks on every repository (Section 3.3), and tournament is set of matches among many participants (Section 3.4).

sections.title: 3.1 PARTICIPANTS AND ENVIRONMENT
sections.content: A participant is pair (m, h), where is the model and is the harness that provides the agent loop, tools, context policy, command execution, and recovery behavior. The same model under two harnesses counts as two participants, each with its own task bank and records. Every duel runs inside Docker container built for one open-source repository pinned to specific commit. The repositorys existing test suite records the original behavior and is re-run on every later artifact (the new feature, the embedded bug, and Blues patch) to detect regressions. Red sessions, validation gates, and scored Blue runs all start from the same image, so every participant works in an identical environment.

sections.title: 3.2 RED AGENT: TASK CREATION
sections.content: Red creates each task in three sessions, and each session is followed by an executable validation gate (Figure 3). Every session starts with fresh context, so session knows only what we pass to 4 Under review as conference paper at ICLR 2027 Figure 3: Three-session task generation. Each of the targets is stored inside slot. Each slot permits at most five attempts: challenge successfully generated within 5 attempts is stored inside its corresponding slot, whereas if it exceeds five attempts, it leaves an exhausted slot. Validation gate ensures the verifiability of the implemented feature. Validation gate ensures the verifiability of the embedded bug. Validation gate ensures the fairness of the embedded bug by verifying the same-system reviewer detects and removes the bug from the new feature. it. For each participant and repository, we request tasks, one per slot. slot allows at most five attempts. The first attempt that passes all three gates is admitted and stored in the participants task bank. If all five attempts fail, the slot is exhausted and stays empty. We never replace an exhausted slot with new one, because creating valid task (implementing feature, embedding bug, writing both test suites, and passing self-repair) is part of the ability we measure. An exhausted slot later counts as missing task in match (Section 3.4). Session A: Feature Implementation Red explores the repository R, picks target module on its own, implements new feature, and writes the feature specification and the feature tests Tf . We denote the resulting feature-only diff by df . To keep participants tasks on one repository diverse, Red is shown the specifications and target files of its earlier admitted tasks there and must pick different module. The validation gate of session requires that the existing test suite Te and generated feature tests Tf pass on df and that the diff and the tests meet minimum size thresholds. Tests that already fail on the pinned commit are recorded and ignored. This gate establishes that the feature is correct before any bug is added, so later failure can be attributed to the bug and not to broken feature. Session B: Bug Embedding fresh Red session receives the feature specification and the diff df . It edits the feature code to embed bug, which gives the final diff d, and writes the bug tests Tb. The validation gate of session requires that (i) applies to the pinned commit and passes lint or compilation; (ii) the build, Te, Tf , and the size checks still pass on d; and (iii) Tb passes on df but fails on d. Condition (ii) ensures that the bug gives Blue no visible failing test. Condition (iii) ensures that Tb tests the bug and not the feature, and that the presence of the bug can be checked by execution. Session C: Blind Self-Repair Deterministic gates of session and show that the embedded bug exists and is hidden, but not that it can be detected and fixed from what reviewer sees. Therefore, fresh instance of the same participant receives only the public bundle pub(C) (i.e., repository, fea5 Under review as conference paper at ICLR 2027 ture specification, pull-request diff, and feature tests), which is exactly what Blue will later receive, and submits revised diff d. The task is admitted only if Te, Tf , and Tb all pass on d, which is the same condition under which Blue wins turn. This keeps unsolvable tasks out, but it also means task can be no harder than its authors own bug-finding ability. We view this as deliberate trade-off between solvability and difficulty. Admitted tasks are saved in bank and reused in every match of tournament, so all opponents face the same tasks from given Red.

sections.content: Blue receives the public bundle pub(C) of task from Reds bank, exactly as the reviewer in Session does (Section 3.2). The bug tests Tb and the bug metadata stay hidden. Blue starts from fresh context in the same container image and is asked to review the pull request as if it came from contributor. The prompt does not say that bug exists. Blue may edit the code, including rewriting the feature, or leave the pull request as it is, and then submits its final diff d. The framework then runs the three test suites on d. sections.title: 3.4 TOURNAMENT
sections.content: A match between participants and is played over set of repositories = {R1, . . . , RR} with tasks per repository. Let Cc,j,i denote the i-th admitted task of participant on repository Rj. For every Rj and every , the match has two turns: plays Blue on CA,j,i, and plays Blue on CB,j,i. match therefore has 2N turns, and each participant plays Red and Blue equally often on the same repositories. If participant admitted fewer than tasks on Rj because its slots were exhausted, each missing task is scored as Blue win without running Blue. We call all other turns contested. Missing tasks thus lower their authors match score. Each turn gives one point to Blue if SBlue = 1 (Eq. 1) and to Red otherwise. participants match score is the sum of its points in both roles. wins the match if QA > QB, loses if QB > QA, and draws otherwise. Following Chatbot Arena (Chiang et al., 2024) and Arena-Lite (Son et al., 2025), SWE-DUEL uses round-robin format in which every pair of participants plays one match. To add new participant to finished tournament of participants, the new participant first creates its own task bank and then plays against only log2 + 1 incumbents, selected with the active sampling rule of Chatbot Arena (Chiang et al., 2024). The incumbents task banks and all earlier match results are reused unchanged, so the number of new matches grows logarithmically with .

We give automatic win to Blue on missing Red challenges so as to avoid survivor bias (dropping weak task creators), and also to consider task creation as SWE capability of the Red agent, not just task solving. Following existing works in arena-style evaluation of LLMs (Chiang et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025; Son et al., 2025), SWE-DUEL reports tournament outcome using BradleyTerry (BT) ratings (Bradley & Terry, 1952). It assigns each participant log-strength βp (centered to zero mean), fitted by maximum likelihood over all match outcomes of Section 3.4 under the model Pr(p beats q) = σ(βp βq) with σ the logistic function and draw counted as half win for each side, from which we report rank probability distributions and 95% confidence intervals using 1,000 bootstrap resamples of matches.

sections.title: 4.3 ADDITIONAL ANALYSIS

To measure this, we re-ran the same check three more times on stratified sample of 44 tournament tasks (4 per participant). Of these, 35 were self-repaired in all three runs, 8 in two, and one in none. The pooled self-repair rate is 91.7% (95% Wilson CI 85.795.3%). Admitted tasks are therefore mostly reliably solvable, and lucky admissions are rare (Appendix I). Bug test case soundness. The sealed bug tests are written by Red, so test that is too specific could incorrectly reject legitimate repair. We manually checked seeded random sample of 50 of the 158 turns that Blue lost only on the bug tests. We found 45 genuine misses, three valid repairs rejected by the test, and two ambiguous cases: 6.0% false-negative rate (95% Wilson CI 2.116.2%). All three false negatives come from two Go JWT tasks whose tests require one specific error type or option (more detail in Appendix G). sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We present SWE-DUEL, an arena in which coding agents test each other. In 1,500-turn tournament among 11 participants, GPT-5.5 with Codex CLI was the strongest solver, repairing 98.3% of the defects it reviewed. Claude Opus 4.8 with mini-swe-agent was the strongest task author, with 27.3% Red win rate. new participant joined with only five matches without changing the existing order. Within one model family, tasks written by the newest version defeated fixed solver far more often than those of older versions, which gives early evidence that task difficulty rises with the authors ability.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: In this work, we used generative AI to generate tasks, and attempt solutions to the tasks for evaluation of AI coding agents. We have not used generative AI tools to conceptualize our framework, propose or refine hypotheses, design research methodology or experiments, implement methods, clean and reformat dataset, support qualitative and thematic data analysis, or interpret results. Using generative AI tools for formulating mathematical claims, providing critical ingredients for proving mathematical claims, assisting in the writing of proofs, or assisting with translation are not applicable to this work. We used generative AI tools for create and polish figures or images, suggest experimental parameters, create and edit software code, and edit and format the paper to improve readability. AI-generated code was manually verified in pair programming sessions by the first and second authors, and was further verified using unit and integration test cases. We take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims or artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: SWE-DUEL is deliberately capable of generating subtle defects in plausible changes to real opensource code, selecting defects that evade the repositorys existing CI and admitting them only when frontier reviewer can nevertheless repair them under blind review. It is therefore an automated generator of CI-evading defects, not merely conventional code-generation benchmark, and its prompts, trajectories, sealed tests, and admitted challenge bank are dual-use artifacts. The observed 27.3% attack success rate of the strongest Red participant against frontier-model reviewers is consequently disclosure-relevant security finding: it demonstrates that apparently plausible, test-passing contributions can retain defects despite automated review, rather than establishing an exploit rate for deployed software. All generation and evaluation in this study ran in isolated local containers at pinned repository revisions. We did not target deployed services, contact maintainers under false pretenses, open pull requests, or submit any generated feature, defect, test, or patch to real repository. If future use of the pipeline reveals an independently existing vulnerability rather than an introduced benchmark defect, we require coordinated disclosure to the affected maintainer before publication. These safeguards do not eliminate the dual-use risk, and we will revisit access decisions if evidence suggests that release would materially increase practical misuse.

sections.title: REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
sections.content: We have open-sourced the SWE-DUEL toolkit (Minn, 2026c) and the experiment dataset (Minn, 2026a) for reproducibility.

sections.title: A TASK FRESHNESS AND TASK BANK RELEASE POLICY
sections.content: The same task cannot remain both public and unseen. In SWE-DUEL, generated bank is static within tournament so every opponent faces controlled, reusable tasks; freshness is renewed across tournaments by generating new task bank. Full publication of replicated results would enable exact external replay, but it would both make the tasks unsuitable for future unseen-task claims. We encourage the generating of new task bank for each replication study to limit the possibility of the released tasks from previous replication studies leaking into the training data of newer LLMs. Any disclosed task bank should be marked retired and cannot support evaluation of models released in the future, and other unseen-task-related works.

sections.title: D ADDITIONAL EXPERIMENTAL DETAIL
sections.content: D.1 HARNESS SETUP All participants receives an initial step budget of 50 harness steps. The 50-step initial ceiling applies separately to Red feature generation, Red bug embedding, blind self-review, and each Blue tasksolving sessions. Each of the sessions are also subject to 30-minute wall-clock limit. If required artifacts remain missing, up to three recovery turns of six steps each is given to the participant. In this work, we choose mini-swe-agent (Yang et al., 2024), Codex CLI (OpenAI, 2026b), and Claude Code (Anthropic, 2026b), all of which are popular harnesses that post strong performances across various coding benchmarks. Note that different models use different amount of compute resources, especially depending on the accompanying harness. Thus, the harness step counts do not represent equal compute. Appendix reports token-level compute-controlled analysis. All the agents, validation gates, and turn scorers run in separate Docker container instances of the same repositoryspecific image to ensure consistent environment. The inference temperature for all the models is fixed at 0.2. D.2 MODEL API ACCESS DATES All participants access their models through the OpenRouter API1. Table 5 lists the first and last recorded API access date for each model. The windows span task creation (including failed attempts and blind self-review validation), evaluation in the main and harness-ablation tournaments, and the post-hoc studies of Appendices I, J, and K: the adaptive task difficulty study adds the GLM-5.1 and GLM-5.3 windows (adaptive task creation), and extends the DeepSeek V4 Pro window (fixedreference task solver for the adaptive tasks). They are identical across the harnesses paired with model because all harnesses route to the same OpenRouter endpoint; all dates are in UTC. 1https://openrouter.ai Under review as conference paper at ICLR 2027 Table 5: Per-model API access dates. Each entry gives the first and last recorded model call through the OpenRouter API (UTC). All calls of model use the same OpenRouter model identifier regardless of the paired harness.

sections.content: Algorithm 1 describes the end-to-end procedure encompassing task cache lookup, and turn-based match scoring. The Load(r, Rj, i) procedure returns the ith admitted task for Red participant in bank-index order. sections.title: K SCALING TASK DIFFICULTY WITH TASK GENERATOR CAPABILITY
sections.content: While the fixed reference solver of Appendix removes the solver-field confound, it still compares the participants of different origin that happen to be in the field. Thus, their task difficulties are property of the generated tasks, not that it changing with task authoring capability. We therefore hold the solver fixed and move the task author along known capability axis. Successive versions of one model family are exactly such an axis, so we built three-rung ladder from GLM-5.1 GLM-5.2 GLM-5.3, all running the same mini-swe-agent harness. Each version authored tasks over the same repository field under the identical task generation protocol and validation gates. GLM-5.1 and GLM-5.3 wrote fresh banks (12 and 14 admitted tasks, respectively); the 13 GLM-5.2 tasks are its admitted tasks from the main tournament. We use DeepSeek-V4-Pro with mini-swe-agent as the fixed reference solver for this study, as it is another mid-tier solver whose contested Blue success of .919 sits near the field aggregate of .851, and model outside the ladder family. The fixed-reference solver than then blind-solved every one of the 39 ladder tasks through the exact task-solving path of match sub-turn: same Blue prompt, step and wall-clock budgets, regression and feature test suites, and sealed bugfix oracle. Since the fixed-reference solver had already solved the 13 GLM-5.2 tasks in-match during the main round-robin tournament, those turn records are reused as part of this study. Result. Solver failure rises with the capability frontier  (Table 2)  : 1/12 (8.3%, Wilson 95% [1.5, 35.4]) for GLM-5.1, 0/13 for GLM-5.2, and 6/14 (42.9%, [21.4, 67.4]) for GLM-5.3. The upward trend across the ladder is significant (exact conditional CochranArmitage trend test over the 39 draws, z=2.32, one-sided p=.015), and the newest version is clearly separated from the pooled older ones (6/14 vs. 1/25, Fisher p=.005), while the two older versions are indistinguishable from each other. All seven failures are complete collapses (Blue composite 0.00), and the solver works harder on the tasks it loses (mean 37.3 vs. 31.5 steps), so failures are exhausted budgets ending in broken behavior rather than early give-ups. Composition vs. difficulty. The defect-category mix shifts along the ladder (security vulnerabilities 4 2 7; logic errors 2 9 2), and GLM-5.2s bank is dominated by logic errors that the solver always repaired. Composition alone, however, does not explain the jump: within securityvulnerability tasks only, the older versions tasks never defeat the solver (0/6) while GLM-5.3s do in 5/7 (Fisher p=.016) even though that category was among the most solvable for the full field in main tournament (84.9% Blue success). Admission yield does not explain it either: per-attempt yields are 12/39 (30.8%), 13/32 (40.6%), and 14/37 (37.8%), non-monotonic across the ladder, with the difficulty jump occurring where yield slightly falls. Thus, difficulty rises alongside rather than because of other task generation statistics. Head-to-head tournament among the ladder versions. The fixed solver sits outside the family, so it cannot say how the three versions fare against one another. Thus, we conducted complete roundrobin tournament where every version plays Red and Blue on every repository once per pairing (Figure 4). The head-to-head tournament produces endogenous match-ups which correlated with the ladder. GLM-5.3s tasks defeat GLM-5.1 in 7/14 contested turns and GLM-5.2 in 4/14, while the two older versions almost never defeat anyone (3/50 pooled across their four cells; one-sided exact Fisher against GLM-5.3s 11/28: p=.0004). The newest version is also the strongest solver, conceding 2/25 contested turns to its siblings tasks versus 4/26 for GLM-5.2 and 8/27 for GLM5.1; it won both of its matches (71 and 41 in Red wins) and GLM-5.2 won the third (10), clean 210 sweep of the standings. The sibling readings agree with the fixed-reference solver where they overlap: the outside solver failed on 6/14 of GLM-5.3s tasks, the siblings on 4/14 and 7/14, and on the two older versions tasks no solver in either study concedes more than single turn. Siblings share training lineage and may share blind spots, so the matrix corroborates rather than replaces the fixed-solver measurement. Insights. With solver, harness, repositories, and protocol held fixed, tasks authored by the newest version of the family are an order of magnitude harder for the same solver than the pooled older versions tasks (42.9% vs. 4.0% failure). Together with the trend test, this is direct evidence for the self-scaling property of SWE-DUEL design: as the authoring agents improve, the tasks they produce get harder for fixed solver. One fixed-reference solver (DeepSeek V4 Pro with mini-swe-agent) is the single measuring stick just like Appendix where the rank agreement of ρ=.66 suggests the reading transfers to other mid-tier solvers, and the within-family round-robin (Figure 4) supplies two sibling solvers whose failure rates climb the same way, but siblings share the familys training Under review as conference paper at ICLR 2027 lineage, so they corroborate rather than independently re-measure the ladder. The ladder has three rungs from one model family; such ladders are cheap to extend (the fresh rungs here cost $15.27 total), so the task difficulty scaling trend can be continuously verified as new versions ship. At 12 14 tasks per level and one draw per task at temperature 0.2, adjacent-version resolution is limited (the admission stability study in Appendix measured .917 per-run repair rate, and the two older levels intervals overlap almost entirely), so even though the task difficulty scaling is not strictly per-version monotone, the data still supports it roughly scaling with the capability frontier. ROLE DECOMPOSITION AND CONTESTED-ONLY BT REFITS Role Decomposition. Table 8 separates the two capabilities that the end-to-end match score intentionally combines: Red task generation capability, and Blue task solving capability. Thus, we analyze the task solving-only BT fit of the main round-robin tournament. Coverage is the number of admitted tasks divided by the 15 scheduled repository slots; an unsuccessful chain of 5 attempts counts as one exhausted slot. The task-solving intervals are task-clustered bootstrap intervals. Figure 8 decomposes each system into task creation and task solving. Nemotron-3-Ultras contested Red win rate is 10/70, but nine of the ten wins come from one of its seven admitted tasks. bootstrap draw that omits both winning clusters rates the task creator at zero while draw that includes the nine-win task several times is rated near 0.5. Thus, the result is the fields widest task-creation interval, [0.000, 0.450]. Appendix analyzes the responsible task in detail. MissingRed auto-wins are excluded. On preventing saturation. As we have seen in this section, models are generally better at finding bugs and solving tasks than they are at authoring tasks. Plus, the admission of task is contingent upon the task authors task solving capability. Thus, the shrinking gaps in task solving capabilities 33 Under review as conference paper at ICLR 2027 among frontier models could shrink the gaps in their task authoring capabilities, potentially leading to saturation of the arena. Two solutions (one short-term, and one long-term) address this problem: (Short-term, temporary) Appendix shows the 15 repositories used in our experiments. They are selected for being relatively small-sized projects in their respective languages/domains. This is because we need their test suites to be lightweight enough for quick execution of validation gates for the sake of our experiments, and for the agent participants to not face too much difficulty with generating tasks and burn the expensive LLM API resources (Appendix R). Thus, practitioners adopting SWE-DUEL may extend to cover bigger repositories with more complex codebases that has wider surface area for feature generation and more subtle and nuanced bug embedding. This would help better highlight the gap in coding capabilities of different frontier models, and prevent saturation of the arena that would otherwise be confined to the same set of 15 lightweight repositories. (Long-term, permanent) future extension of this work could focus on the solvability checks that does not require blind self-reviewing by the task author, and thus is not capped by the task solving capability of the task author. For example, the solvability check gate could involve the privileged information such as informing the self-review session about the existence of the bug, or to look for the specific type of the bug. This would still prove the bug is fair and solvable, but now the task author has more leeway to embed more subtle and challenging bugs that no longer needs to be detected and fixed by the blind self-review session. Nine of its ten contested Red wins arise from one admitted artifact, task 71a623dd on the Go gorilla/csrf repository. This section analyzes the artifact of the task and its ten persisted solving runs to characterize what its difficulty measures. Task details. The feature adds SkipPaths option: request paths equal to configured path skip CSRF validation exactly, and paths beneath configured path ending in slash skip by prefix. The sealed defect is one-condition change in the prefix matcher: the request path must additionally be strictly longer than the cleaned skip path, so request equal to the configured prefix itself (for instance POST /webhook/ under skip path /webhook/) fails validation instead of being skipped. The sealed bug test requires the lenient reading; no visible signal does. The visible feature suite enforces the strict behavior for the unslashed path (/webhook must be rejected) and accepts only strict descendants, and the PRs own doc comment over-claims the lenient semantics, contradicting those tests. solver must therefore settle specification conflict in which every visible signal corroborates the defective behavior. The ten solving runs. One participant solved the task (GPT-5.5 with Codex CLI) while the other nine lost. Each of the 9 losses is latent bug ship (existing and feature suites pass, only the sealed suite fails), and one of the nine also appears in the audit sample of Appendix as genuine miss (solving run 56210ac0). Eight of the nine explicitly inspected or reasoned about the strict-length condition; five filed lowor info-severity findings that framed the discrepancy as documentation error rather than functional one. Only one solver (GLM-5.2) never mentions the matching condition at all. The single success is the one solving run that separated the two path forms (the unslashed path must stay protected while the prefix path itself must skip) and added its own matcher tests; it too labeled the issue low-severity, but repaired it. The task contains genuine bug. The manual audit reveals the sampled solving run is true failure of the participants in identifying the bug, rather than an unsound bug-test oracle. But it does not test whether Blue solver can locate the hidden bug, as most solvers located the exact condition according to the manual inspection of the Blue agents reasoning traces.
